summary: Specifies the Online Certificate Status Protocol, which lets a client ask a server about the current status of a digital certificate without downloading certificate revocation lists. It was replaced by RFC 6960 and updated by RFC 6277.

eli5.summary: Instead of checking a long list of cancelled ID cards, you just ask the office whether this one is still good and get a quick yes or no.

questions: how to check if a certificate is revoked
subtitle: Ask a server whether one certificate is still good, instead of downloading a whole revocation list.

tldr.problem: Checking a certificate against a periodic CRL can be too slow for cases that need timely revocation information, such as high-value funds transfers or large stock trades.
tldr.mechanism: An OCSP client sends a status request for a specific certificate to an OCSP responder, which returns a signed response saying good, revoked or unknown.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2560 was obsoleted by RFC 6960 and updated by RFC 6277, so new work should use RFC 6960.

today: RFC 2560 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 6960 and updated by RFC 6277. Use RFC 6960 for the current definition of OCSP.

sections.title: Protocol Overview and Messages
sections.content:
The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) lets an application find out the revocation state of an identified certificate. It can replace or supplement checking a periodic CRL. The RFC gives high-value funds transfers and large stock trades as examples where timely information may be needed.

An OCSP client sends a status request to an OCSP responder and suspends acceptance of the certificate until the responder answers. A request carries a protocol version, a service request, a target certificate identifier and optional extensions. The responder checks that the message is well formed, that it is configured to provide the service, and that the request has the information it needs. If any check fails it returns an error message; otherwise it returns a definitive response.

Messages are defined in ASN.1 and signed data is encoded with DER. A request is an OCSPRequest holding a TBSRequest and an optional signature. Each entry in the request list names a certificate with a CertID: a hash algorithm, a hash of the issuer's name, a hash of the issuer's public key, and the certificate's serial number. The key hash is used as well as the name hash because two CAs may choose the same name but will not normally share a public key.

A response always has a responseStatus. When the status is an error, no response bytes are included. A successful response carries a type and the response itself. All responders MUST be able to produce, and all clients MUST be able to process, the id-pkix-ocsp-basic type. A basic response has the responder's ID, a producedAt time, and one SingleResponse per certificate, followed by a signature.

Each SingleResponse gives the certificate ID, a status of good, revoked or unknown, thisUpdate, an optional nextUpdate and optional extensions. A revoked status includes the revocation time and optionally a reason.
sections.eli5:
A shop that is unsure about a gift card phones the issuer and waits for an answer before accepting it.

The question is a slip with the card's number and who issued it. The answer is a signed note that says good, cancelled, or never heard of it.

sections.title: Status Values, Errors and Times
sections.content:
The good state means at least that the certificate is not revoked. It does not necessarily mean the certificate was ever issued, or that the response time falls within its validity interval. revoked covers a certificate revoked permanently or temporarily (on hold). unknown means the responder does not know the certificate. If a responder knows a CA's private key was compromised, it MAY return revoked for all certificates issued by that CA.

Error responses are not signed. The defined statuses are successful (0), malformedRequest (1), internalError (2), tryLater (3), sigRequired (5) and unauthorized (6); value 4 is not used.

Three times matter. thisUpdate is when the status is known to be correct, nextUpdate is the time at or before which newer information will be available, and producedAt is when the responder signed the response. If nextUpdate is not set, newer information is available all the time. Responders MAY pre-produce signed responses.
sections.eli5: The answer has a date stamp saying when it was true and when to ask again. If the office is busy or confused, it sends a plain note instead, and that note is not signed.

sections.title: Who May Sign and What Clients Check
sections.content:
All definitive responses SHALL be signed. The signing key must belong to the CA that issued the certificate, a Trusted Responder whose key the requester trusts, or a CA Designated Responder (Authorized Responder). A designated responder holds a certificate issued directly by the CA that contains id-kp-OCSPSigning in its extendedKeyUsage extension.

Before accepting a signed response, a client SHALL confirm six things: the certificate matches the request, the signature is valid, the signer is the intended recipient of the request, the signer is currently authorized, thisUpdate is sufficiently recent, and, when present, nextUpdate is later than the current time.

A CA has three ways to deal with revocation checking of an authorized responder's own certificate. It can include the id-pkix-ocsp-nocheck extension so clients trust the responder for the certificate's lifetime. It can name a CRL or other method to check. Or it can specify nothing, leaving the choice to the client's local policy.
sections.eli5: Only the card issuer, or someone the issuer officially names, may answer. The shop checks the stamp and the date before believing the answer.

sections.title: Extensions
sections.content:
Support for every extension is optional for clients and responders. The critical flag SHOULD NOT be set on request extensions, and unrecognized extensions MUST be ignored unless they are marked critical and not understood. The RFC defines these:

  • Nonce (id-pkix-ocsp-nonce): binds a request to its response to prevent replay attacks.
  • CRL References: tells which CRL a revoked certificate was found on, by URL, CRL number or time.
  • Acceptable Response Types: lets a client list the response types it understands.
  • Archive Cutoff: shows how far back a responder keeps revocation information. With a 7-year retention policy, the value is the production time minus 7 years.
  • CRL Entry Extensions: the extensions from RFC 2459 section 5.3 are also supported as single extensions.
  • Service Locator: lets a server route a request to the server authoritative for the certificate.
sections.eli5: Extras you can staple to the slip, like a secret number that proves the answer is for this very question.

sections.title: Certificates, Algorithms and OCSP over HTTP
sections.content:
CAs that support OCSP MUST allow the AuthorityInfoAccess extension in certificates to carry a URI with the id-ad-ocsp access method. The location also defines the transport, such as HTTP. A client may instead configure the responder location locally.

Clients SHALL be able to process responses signed with DSA keys, and SHOULD also handle RSA signatures. Responders SHALL support the SHA1 hashing algorithm.

Appendix A describes HTTP use. Requests under 255 bytes after encoding MAY use GET so that HTTP caching works; larger ones, or those where caching does not matter, SHOULD use POST. POST uses the content type application/ocsp-request and responses use application/ocsp-response. Where privacy is needed, TLS/SSL or another lower-layer protocol MAY be used.
sections.eli5: The certificate says where to ask. The question is usually sent like a web request, short ones in the address and long ones in the body.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
OCSP only helps if clients can reach the status service. If they cannot, they could fall back to CRL processing.

A flood of queries is a denial-of-service risk, made worse because producing a signature slows response generation. Because error responses are unsigned, an attacker can also send false errors. Pre-computed responses allow replay attacks: an old good response replayed after the certificate was revoked but before its expiry. Requests do not name their target responder, so a request can be replayed to many responders. Finally, misconfigured HTTP caches can produce unexpected results.
sections.eli5: Bad guys could swamp the office with questions, fake a busy signal, or show an old yes after the card was cancelled.

messages.label: OCSPRequest
messages.note: Names the certificate by issuer name hash, issuer key hash and serial number.

messages.label: OCSPResponse
messages.note: Signed status: good, revoked or unknown. Error statuses are unsigned.
